blocks.text: And Lucian in the Cock, to a greedy rich man: Οἴμωζε, καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖ, καὶ ὅμοιος γίγνου τὸ χρῶμα τῷ χρυσῷ, προσετηκὼς αὐτῷ [oimōze, kai agrypnei, kai homoios gignou to chrōma tō chrysō, prosetēkōs autō]; Lament and keep watch, and, wasting away over your gold, become like it in colour. Now, if you ask why this golden colour is attributed to doves, Kimchi answers: שיש בכנפי היונה נוצה שהמצהבת כזהב, In the wings of doves there is plumage yellow like gold: namely in the wings of the younger birds, after they have left the nest. The Talmudists observe the same of turtledoves, and say that from this one learns when they are fit or unfit for sacrifice. For since the Law commands that of doves only the young, and of turtledoves only the adults, be offered, they hold that the former become unfit for sacrifice, and the latter fit, precisely when the feathers begin to turn yellow like gold. The words are in the tractate Cholin, chapter 1, folio 22b: מאימתי התורים כשרים משיצהיבו מאימתי בני יונה פסולים משיצהיבו When are turtledoves (for offering) fit? From the time they begin to turn yellow like gold. When are young doves (for offering) unfit? From the time they begin to turn yellow like gold. And on the word משיצהיבו the Gloss has: שיהא כנפי גופן גדולים ואדומים ומזהיבים כזהב, because the feathers of the body become large and red, and yellow like gold. And somewhat earlier: תחילה הציהב כשמתחילין לצהב כנפים שמסביבות צוארן The beginning of the yellowing is when the feathers they have around the neck begin to turn yellow like gold. So also Maimonides in Issure Mizbeach ch. 3, §2: והתורים כשרים משיזהבו Turtledoves are fit for offering from the time they have a golden colour. Where the Gloss is the same as in the Talmud above. But the necks of doves too, when facing the sun, shine with a golden colour. The Philosopher, in the book On Colours: Οἱ τῶν περιστερῶν τράχηλοι, καὶ τῶν ὑδάτων οἱ σταλαγμοὶ φαίνονται χρυσοειδεῖς, τοῦ φωτὸς ἀνακλωμένου [Hoi tōn peristerōn trachēloi, kai tōn hydatōn hoi stalagmoi phainontai chrysoeideis, tou phōtos anaklōmenou]. The necks of doves and drops of water appear to be of a golden colour when the light is reflected. Others write only that they gleam with various colours. Lucretius, book 2, line 800:

As the plumage of doves appears in the sun, which, set about the nape, crowns the neck: [II, 536] for at times it comes to be red with bright fire-bronze, at times, by a certain way of seeing, it seems to mingle green emeralds with sky-blue.

Philo, in the book On Drunkenness: Τὸν αὐχένα τῆς περιστερᾶς ἐν ἡλιακαῖς αὐγαῖς οὐ κατενόησας μυρίας χρωμάτων ἀλλάττοντα ἰδέας; ἢ οὐχὶ φοινικοῦν, καὶ κυανοῦν, πυροπόν τε, καὶ ἀνθρακοειδὲς, ἔτι τε ὠχρὸν, καὶ ἐρυθρὸν, καὶ ἄλλα παντόδαπα ἴσχει χρώματα, ὧν οὐδὲ τὰς κλήσεις ῥάδιον ἀπομνημονεῦσαι [Ton auchena tēs peristeras en hēliakais augais ou katenoēsas myrias chrōmatōn allattonta ideas? ē ouchi phoinikoun, kai kyanoun, pyropon te, kai anthrakoeides, eti te ōchron, kai erythron, kai alla pantodapa ischei chrōmata, hōn oude tas klēseis rhadion apomnēmoneusai]. Have you never seen a dove's neck in the sun's rays varied into countless colours? Does it not have crimson, and sky-blue, and the colours of fire-bronze and of carbuncle, and pale, and red, and colours of every other kind, whose mere names it would not be easy to recount? This Eustathius copied almost word for word in the Hexaemeron, page 29. Nero, in Seneca, Natural Questions book 1, ch. 5:
The necks of Cytherea's dove shine as it moves.

Pliny, book 10, chapter 26: Doves have a certain sense even of glory. You would think they know their own colours and the ordered variety of them. And book 37, chapter 5: The Carchedonian, etc. uncertain in colour, and like the feathers of the green in peacocks' tails and on the necks of doves. Ausonius, on ducks, Epistle 3:
Whom iridescent plumage has painted with varied colour, rivals of doves in their necks.

But these colours are only apparent. Thus in Martianus, book 2, [col. 11] Arcesilas, gazing at the neck of doves and moved by this uncertainty of variation, began to build up further his doctrine of ἀκαταληψία [akatalēpsia]. And Carneades, to prove that our senses are uncertain, brought forward the necks of doves, which change colour at every turn. So Jerome attests in his letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem. But Oppian, in book 1 of the Cynegetica, taught that the young even in the egg can be marked with various colours, and real ones at that: namely if, when the females are about to mate, there are set before them

— — — — — δαίδαλα πολλὰ Εἵματα πορφύρεα· ταὶ δὲ κλιδὸν ὄσσε βαλοῦσαι, Θυμὸν ἰαινόμεναι τίκτουσ᾽ ἁλιπόρφυρα τέκνα, [— — — — — daidala polla heimata porphyrea; tai de klidon osse balousai, thymon iainomenai tiktous' haliporphyra tekna,]

many richly wrought purple garments: and they, casting sidelong glances at them and delighted in mind, bring forth purple young. I cite this the more gladly because by a similar art Jacob obtained parti-coloured sheep for himself.
